title: MIT's Robotic Insect Learns Backflips with AI, Gets 450% Faster
summary: A robot the size of a microcassette and lighter than a paperclip is now doing backflips in midair. Engineers at MIT have developed an AI controller that boosts the speed of their insect-scale flying robot by 450 percent and its acceleration by 250 percent. The robot can complete 10 consecutive somersaults in just 11 seconds, even when wind tries to knock it off course. Its wings are powered by soft artificial muscles that flap incredibly fast. But the real breakthrough is its 'brain'—a two-part AI control system. The first part uses a model-predictive controller, which predicts the robot's movements and plans complex maneuvers like flips and sharp turns. The second part ensures the robot can handle uncertainty and recover from small errors. 'If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times, the robot will just crash,' says Jonathan How, a co-senior author. 'We need robust flight control.' This advance could let these robots navigate through narrow spaces in disaster zones, like collapsed buildings after earthquakes, where larger drones can't fit. 'We want to use these robots in scenarios that traditional quadcopters would have trouble flying into,' says Kevin Chen, head of MIT's Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory. 'Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance is comparable to insects.' The research, published in Science Advances, is a step toward agile rescue robots that mimic the speed and agility of real insects. In the future, such robots might also inspect dangerous industrial sites or search for survivors in rubble, thanks to their ability to squeeze through gaps and recover from midair tumbles. For now, the MIT team is focused on making the control system even more robust, so the tiny robot can handle unpredictable winds and tight spaces without crashing. The goal is a robot that flies as well as a real insect—fast, agile, and nearly impossible to knock off course.
why_it_matters: Tiny flying robots that can survive tumbles and squeeze through gaps could change how search-and-rescue teams work after disasters, where today the bottleneck is control software rather than hardware. It also shows how AI is being used to solve physical problems, so the engineers of the next decade will need robotics and machine-learning skills together.

background_read: MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a science and engineering university in the United States) has been building insect-scale flying robots for years; an earlier famous project, Harvard's RoboBee, proved that a machine lighter than a paperclip could get off the ground at all.

The hard part has never been the wings — it is the control. Because these robots are so small and light, a tiny puff of air can flip one over, and a small error grows with every flap, much like a wobbling bicycle.

The new controller works a bit like a sports coach: the model-predictive part plans the whole flip in advance, while the second part corrects mistakes in real time, similar to how your body adjusts when you stumble.

The study appeared in Science Advances (a peer-reviewed science journal where researchers publish their results), and the MIT team's longer-term goal is rescue work: after an earthquake, robots this small could slip through cracks in collapsed concrete that no ordinary drone could enter.

perspectives.description: They see a breakthrough that could let swarms of cheap robots crawl through rubble after earthquakes, reaching survivors that ordinary drones and heavy machines cannot. The 450 percent speed gain and repeated flips suggest the control problem — long the real barrier — is finally being cracked.

They point out that 11 seconds of backflips in a lab is far from a real mission. Battery life, dust, radio contact, cost and the sheer chaos of a collapsed building are all unsolved, and a robot that crashes when small errors build up may be too fragile to trust in a life-or-death search.

Roboticists have copied insects for decades because evolution already solved flight at small scales, and progress has always been stepwise: first getting airborne, then controlling flight, then autonomy. This work fits that pattern — a control milestone rather than a finished product.

The next questions are robustness, onboard sensing and swarms coordinating with each other. If tiny fliers become reliable, they could also inspect pipelines, bridges and other dangerous industrial sites — raising new questions about how much small flying robots should be allowed to watch.
